notes: Lesson on F=ma. Structure: real-world hook (car acceleration) → definition of force → Newton's 2nd law statement → formula → derivation → worked example with calculation → demonstration video → usage conditions → practice problems. Rich mixed-media lesson.

units.label: Title: Newton's Second Law of Motion
Hook: car accelerating (image)
units.content_summary: Photo of a car accelerating on a road. Caption: 'What factors determine how quickly a car accelerates?' Sets up the central question of the lesson.

units.label: Learning Objectives (text)
units.content_summary: Objectives: state Newton's second law; use F=ma to solve problems; describe relationship between force, mass, and acceleration; give real-world examples.

units.label: Review: definition of force (text)
units.content_summary: Brief review: a force is a push or pull on an object. Forces have magnitude (measured in Newtons) and direction (vector). Net force is the vector sum of all forces.

units.label: Newton's Second Law statement (text)
units.content_summary: Statement: The acceleration of an object depends on the net force acting on the object and the object's mass. Greater force → greater acceleration. Greater mass → less acceleration. F = ma (Newton, 1687).

units.label: Force-mass-acceleration diagram (image)
units.content_summary: Three-part diagram: (1) same force, different masses → larger mass has less acceleration; (2) same mass, different forces → larger force has more acceleration. Visually encodes the F=ma relationship.

units.label: Formula: F = ma with unit definitions (text)
units.content_summary: Formal formula: F = m × a. Units: F in Newtons (N = kg·m/s²), m in kilograms (kg), a in meters per second squared (m/s²). Shows algebraic rearrangements: a = F/m, m = F/a.

units.label: Video: Newton's Second Law demonstration
units.content_summary: Video demonstration using a cart on a track with varying masses and forces. Shows experimentally that doubling the force doubles the acceleration (constant mass) and doubling the mass halves the acceleration (constant force).

units.label: Worked Example: car acceleration calculation (text)
units.content_summary: Problem: a 1200 kg car experiences a net force of 3600 N. Find its acceleration. Solution: a = F/m = 3600/1200 = 3 m/s². Full worked solution with unit analysis.

units.label: Worked Example: find force given mass and acceleration (text)
units.content_summary: Problem: a 5 kg box accelerates at 2 m/s². What net force acts on it? Solution: F = 5 × 2 = 10 N. Includes diagram of the box with force arrow.

units.label: Force diagram for Example 2 (image)
units.content_summary: Free-body diagram of 5 kg box with a 10 N force arrow pointing right and acceleration arrow. Labels show F=10N, m=5kg, a=2m/s².

units.label: Usage condition: Newton's 2nd Law applies to net force (text)
units.content_summary: Important clarification: F in F=ma is the NET force (resultant of all forces). If forces cancel (object at rest or constant velocity), net F=0 and a=0. This is Newton's 1st Law territory.

units.label: Practice problems: F=ma calculations (text)
units.content_summary: Four practice problems: find a given F and m; find F given m and a; find m given F and a; real-world scenario (rocket launch). Students apply F=ma in all three rearrangements.

units.label: Lesson root: Newton's Second Law lesson
